questions.title: Which structure is NOT part of the basal ganglia?
questions.question: Which of the following deep grey-matter structures is NOT one of the basal ganglia?

explanations.A: Correct. The tuber cinereum is part of the hypothalamus, the median-eminence region of the floor of the third ventricle, from which the infundibulum (pituitary stalk) descends. It is functionally and anatomically distinct from the basal ganglia, despite its similarly deep location. Naming it among the basal ganglia is a classic distractor that exploits this superficial similarity in position.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The caudate nucleus, together with the putamen, forms the neostriatum, one of the basal ganglia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The putamen is part of the neostriatum and is one of the basal ganglia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The globus pallidus (paleostriatum) is one of the basal ganglia.

questions.learning_objective: State that the tuber cinereum is a hypothalamic structure and is not one of the basal ganglia.

questions.title: Through which mechanism does a brain tumour classically cause headache?
questions.question: A patient with a newly diagnosed brain tumour reports headache that is worse on waking and aggravated by coughing or straining. Through which mechanism does the tumour classically produce this headache?

options.A: Raised intracranial pressure and traction on pain-sensitive intracranial structures
options.B: Direct pain sensation from the brain parenchyma itself
options.C: Referred pain from pain-sensitive extracranial structures such as the scalp and sinuses

explanations.A: Correct. A brain tumour classically causes headache through intracranial mechanisms — mass effect raising intracranial pressure, obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow (hydrocephalus), and traction or distortion of pain-sensitive intracranial structures such as the dura mater, large blood vessels and venous sinuses. This is why the headache is classically worse in the morning or on waking, and aggravated by coughing, straining or bending, reflecting further transient rises in intracranial pressure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Brain parenchyma itself is insensitive to pain; the headache arises from traction on the surrounding pain-sensitive dura and vessels, not from the tumour tissue itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Referred pain from extracranial structures is the mechanism of extracranial headache (e.g. from otitis media or sinus disease), the mechanistic counterpart to, not the cause of, this intracranial tumour's headache.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Scalp muscle contraction is implicated in tension-type headache, an extracranial mechanism unrelated to the intracranial mass effect of a brain tumour.

questions.learning_objective: State that a brain tumour causes headache through intracranial mechanisms, as opposed to an extracranial cause.
